title: You Swear You Blocked Background Voices, Yet Your Own Mouth Followed the Ignored Ear

acts.name: The 1964 Oxford Dichotic Ear-Swap Mystery
sentences: You think your brain mutes background voices to zero!
But one whispered name across a loud room grabs you!
the turning point came with the Oxford ear swap study.
The breakdown happened in silence with strict filter theories.
Donald Broadbent claimed an early switch blocks ignored words.
At twenty-four, Anne Treisman doubted that rigid switch.
In nineteen sixty-four, she wired listeners to two audio tracks.
Listeners repeated every right-ear word out loud.
They ignored the left ear — and that wasn't the strangest part.

acts.name: When Meaning Jumps Into the Ignored Ear
sentences: What happens if the story jumps into the ignored ear?
Midway through a sentence, Treisman swapped the two audio tracks.
Random words suddenly poured into the focused right ear.
Meanwhile the story jumped straight into the ignored left ear!
Did listeners keep repeating right-ear nonsense like machines?
Volunteers blurted two words from the ignored left ear!
Meaning pulled their voices across before they noticed.
Most listeners had zero clue their speech hopped ears.
Defending an all-or-nothing mute switch was a total nightmare.

acts.name: The Dimmer Knob & Hair-Trigger Words
sentences: Instead of a dead switch, Treisman proposed a smooth dimmer.
Focused voices enter at one hundred percent, like a bright stage lamp.
Ignored voices drop to ten percent, like a turned radio dial.
How can a quiet trickle still trigger your own name?
Your auditory cortex, your hearing center, passes that quiet trickle onward.
Next, Wernicke's area, your language decoder, keeps urgent words on hair triggers.
Your own name and fire alarms need almost zero volume.
But here's the twist: could dimmed meaning cross another language?

acts.name: Bilingual Meaning & The Late-Selection Extreme
sentences: Treisman tested fluent speakers of both English and French.
They repeated an English story entering their right ear.
Quietly, a French translation played inside the ignored left ear.
Would a dimmed foreign voice vanish into background noise?
Bilingual listeners spotted that both ears told the same tale!
Primed concepts recognized their twin across two languages.
Rival scholars soon swung to the opposite extreme.
They claimed your brain decodes every voice in town.

acts.name: 1967 Ruler-Tap Showdown: 87% Versus 8%
sentences: Does your mind really decode every background voice around you?
In nineteen sixty-seven, Treisman and Gina Geffen settled that fight.
Listeners tapped a desk ruler whenever target words appeared.
Focused ears caught eighty-seven percent, like a wide fishing net.
Ignored ears caught just eight percent, like a narrow keyhole slot.
Your parietal cortex, your spatial map, shifts focus when alarms fire.
Surprised every scientist watching
How can you use this dimmer rule in noisy rooms?

acts.name: The Name-First Communication Rule
sentences: Never start an urgent message with the key number first.
Unprimed numbers hit a dimmed ear and bounce right off.
Speak the listener's first name before anything else!
Pause briefly so their name trips that hair-trigger switch.
Now their focus dial swings up to full listening strength.
Hospital teams and flight crews use that exact sequence daily.
One spoken name opens the door before vital facts arrive.
That biological lesson explains selective focus dims the world without ever going deaf.
